hook.text: Three processes are ready. There is one CPU. Who goes first?

burst.text: Each needs the CPU for one stretch of work, its CPU burst. Here, twenty-four, three, and three milliseconds.

tat.text: Two numbers judge a schedule. Turnaround time is when you finish, minus when you arrived.

wt.text: Waiting time is turnaround minus your burst: the time you sat ready, but not running.

wtEx.text: Arrive at two, need nine, finish at twenty-six. Turnaround, twenty-four. Waiting, fifteen.

fcfs.text: The simplest rule is first come, first served. P one arrived first, so P one runs.

fcfs2.text: And runs. And runs. Twenty-four milliseconds. P two and P three only need three each, but they wait.

fcfs3.text: P two waits twenty-four. P three waits twenty-seven. The average waiting time is seventeen.

convoy.text: Short jobs stuck behind a long one. That is the convoy effect.

swap.text: Now the same three arrive in a different order: P two, P three, then P one.

swap2.text: Waiting times six, zero and three. The average drops to three. Same work, same rule, very different result.

sjfQ.text: So why not always run the shortest job first?

sjf.text: That is S J F, shortest job first. Four processes need six, eight, seven, and three.

sjf2.text: The shortest goes first: P four, then P one, then P three, then P two.

sjf3.text: Waiting times three, sixteen, nine and zero. The average is seven, the lowest any order can give.

catch.text: The catch: the OS cannot see the future. It does not know how long the next burst will be. It can only estimate it.

starve.text: And a long job can starve, while short ones keep arriving.

non.text: Both rules are nonpreemptive. Once a process has the CPU, it keeps it until it finishes or blocks.

ex5.text: S J F: minimum average wait, unknown bursts.
